newsitem.title: UK: OIl markets barely budge as OPEC rolls over quotas.
newsitem.headline: OIl markets barely budge as OPEC rolls over quotas.

text.p: The world oil market barely budged on Thursday after OPEC ministers agreed at a meeting in Vienna to freeze output into the first half of next year and support robust prices.

International benchmark crude oil Brent Blend from the North Sea for January delivery traded 14 cents higher at $22.86 a barrel after news from Vienna that the widely anticipated rollover of current production was approved.
"It's not a surprise. It's what the market was expecting and it was already factored in," a futures trader said.

Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) Secretary-General Rilwanu Lukman said after the 11-member producer group ended its meeting that there was agreement to keep output at 25.03 million barrels per day (bpd) until June 1997, when the group will meet again.
OPEC raised its ceiling by 800,000 bpd last June to make way for Iraq, which had been expected to resume oil exports in September for the first time since the Gulf War of 1991.

Even the possibility of a return of Iraqi crude oil exports in a matter of weeks failed to bring out the bears in a winter market characterised by lower than normal crude oil and heating oil stocks in consumer countries.

Such is the market's hunger for crude oil at present that it has been absorbing additional barrels from OPEC members producing above their quotas without a detrimental impact on prices, which remain some $3 a barrel above year-ago levels.
This was largely because refineries allowed inventories to run low on the assumption Iraq would return to the market during the fourth quarter of this year and that non-OPEC supply would rise.
Neither happened and demand was stronger than forecast, allowing OPEC to reap the benefit of a price windfall without lifting a finger.
Oil traders said the pact to keep the OPEC output ceiling at 25.03 million bpd would underpin winter oil markets and offset any downward pressure from a resumption of Iraqi exports.
"OPEC are getting much better at taking the temperature of the market," said Bob Finch, the head of trading at Vitol SA, the world's biggest independent oil trading and refining company.

Earlier this week Iraq and the United Nations reached agreement on an "oil-for-food" deal that will allow Baghdad to sell $2 billion in oil over six months to buy food and medicines. The agreement is renewable.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) in Paris expects the call on OPEC oil to be 26.5 million bpd in the first quarter of 1997, compared to OPEC output of less than 26.0 million in recent months. This should allow room for most of the Iraqi oil at least during the winter months.
But analysts said the additional barrels could weigh on the low demand seasons in the second and third quarters. Crude oil prices in dollars per barrel:
